name: The Explanatory Gap
statement: Even a full account of the brain seems to leave unexplained why any of it feels like anything.
statementAccent: why any of it feels like anything
meaning: The explanatory gap is the difficulty, or apparent impossibility, of explaining how and why physical processes in the brain give rise to subjective, phenomenal conscious experience. The term was coined by the philosopher Joseph Levine in his 1983 paper Materialism and Qualia: The Explanatory Gap. The idea is that even a complete physical or functional account of the brain seems to leave unexplained why that processing is accompanied by any felt experience at all, why there is something it is like to undergo it; there is a gap between the physical facts and the phenomenal facts of what experience feels like. Levine's classic illustration contrasts two identity statements. The statement that water is H2O is explanatorily satisfying, because water's observable properties can be derived from the properties of H2O. But the statement that pain is the firing of C-fibers, even if it is true, does not have the same explanatory force: it does not explain why that neural state feels the way it does, or feels like anything at all. Levine framed the gap as primarily epistemic, a matter of our ability to explain and understand, rather than necessarily an ontological gap about what exists, and he was himself somewhat sympathetic to physicalism. The explanatory gap is closely related to the hard problem of consciousness and remains an influential challenge to reductive explanations of the mind.
mechanism: The explanatory gap emerges when we compare successful reductive explanations elsewhere in science with the attempt to explain consciousness. A good reductive explanation, such as identifying water with H2O, satisfies us because it lets us see why the higher-level phenomenon has the features it does: given the molecular structure of H2O and the laws of physics and chemistry, we can understand why water is liquid at room temperature, boils at a certain point, and dissolves salt. The identity closes the explanatory question. Now consider a proposed psychophysical identity, such as that pain is the firing of C-fibers. Even if this identity is true and the neural state is always present with pain, it does not seem to explain why that state should feel painful, or feel like anything at all; one can apparently grasp the full physical story while the question of why it is accompanied by that particular felt quality remains open. This asymmetry is the explanatory gap: physical explanations of consciousness lack the explanatory force that reductive explanations have in other domains. Levine emphasized that the gap is in the first instance epistemic, a limit on our ability to explain and understand the connection, and he distinguished this from the stronger ontological claim that consciousness is therefore non-physical, since the explanatory difficulty could persist even if physicalism is true. The gap thus poses a challenge without by itself settling the metaphysics.

variants.name: Epistemic versus ontological
variants.text: The distinction between a gap in our ability to explain and a gap in what actually exists, with Levine stressing the former.

variants.name: The physicalist responses
variants.text: Replies that the gap is merely conceptual, such as the phenomenal concepts strategy, and illusionist denials.

whyItMatters: The explanatory gap is one of the most influential formulations in the philosophy of consciousness, giving precise shape to the difficulty of explaining subjective experience in physical terms. By showing that even a true identification of a mental state with a brain state, such as pain with C-fiber firing, lacks the explanatory force that reductive identities have elsewhere in science, Joseph Levine crystallized the sense that consciousness poses a special explanatory challenge, one that ordinary scientific reduction seems unable to meet. The concept is a cornerstone of the debate over physicalism and closely allied to David Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness, Thomas Nagel's question of what it is like to be a bat, and the knowledge argument, together forming the core case that experience resists physical explanation. Levine's careful distinction between the epistemic gap, about our ability to explain, and any ontological gap, about what exists, has itself been important, since it frames whether the difficulty is merely a limit on our understanding or a sign that consciousness is not physical. The explanatory gap continues to structure discussion in philosophy of mind and consciousness science.

limits: The explanatory gap is influential, but its interpretation is contested, and Levine himself was careful about what it shows. He framed it as primarily an epistemic gap, about our ability to explain and understand, rather than an ontological gap about what exists, so the difficulty could persist even if physicalism is true, and he was comparatively sympathetic to physicalism; treating the gap as directly proving that consciousness is non-physical goes beyond his claim. Physicalists argue the gap is merely epistemic or conceptual, a limit on our understanding that may eventually close, and appeal to the phenomenal concepts strategy, holding that our special concepts of experience create the appearance of a gap without any gap in reality. Illusionists deny there is robust phenomenal consciousness to explain at all.
misreadings: The explanatory gap does not by itself prove that consciousness is non-physical; Levine framed it as an epistemic gap about our ability to explain, not an ontological one about what exists, and he leaned toward physicalism. It is not a claim that the psychophysical identity is false, but that even a true identity fails to explain why the state feels a certain way. And it is not agreed to be unbridgeable, since physicalists argue it is merely conceptual and may close, so treating the gap as proving dualism, as denying the identity, or as a settled permanent gap, misreads Levine's primarily epistemic challenge.
origin: A concept coined by the philosopher Joseph Levine in his 1983 paper Materialism and Qualia: The Explanatory Gap, marking the difficulty of explaining why physical brain processes are accompanied by subjective experience.
